metaData.originalTitle: Inside the Ludicrous， Deadly Serious Plan to Take Over Greenland
metaData.title: Inside the Ludicrous， Deadly Serious Plan to Take Over Greenland
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: This New Yorker investigation reveals how Donald Trump's fantasy of annexing Greenland was pursued by a small group of ideologues and opportunists through covert influence operations, undermining NATO and the post-WWII world order.
metaData.summary: This deeply reported piece by Ben Taub traces the evolution of Donald Trump's obsession with acquiring Greenland from a 2018 dinner-table fantasy into a concerted, multi-pronged campaign during his second term. The article profiles four key figures—Chris Cox (Bikers for Trump founder), Tom Dans (former venture capitalist and Treasury official), Drew Horn (former Special Forces commander), and Jørgen Boassen (a Greenlandic supporter)—who ran private influence operations in Greenland, often without the knowledge of the Danish or Greenlandic governments. It details the secret National Security Council task force (the Greenland Policy Coordination Committee) formed during Trump's first term, which worked to accelerate Greenlandic independence in a way that would increase U.S. control, while simultaneously undermining Denmark. The story culminates in the post-2024 reality where Trump's threats have become official policy, Danish soldiers prepare to blow up runways to deter a U.S. invasion, and the Danish Prime Minister declares the post-WWII world order is over. The piece is a stark examination of how personal whims and informal channels have replaced traditional diplomacy, turning a former ally into a potential target.

mainPoints.point: Trump's Greenland pursuit was driven by personal obsession, not strategic necessity.
mainPoints.explanation: The article traces the idea to a 2018 suggestion from Ronald Lauder, showing how it was amplified by a small group of loyalists and opportunists, not by a consensus of national security experts.

mainPoints.point: A secret NSC task force worked to subvert Denmark and accelerate Greenlandic independence.
mainPoints.explanation: The Greenland Policy Coordination Committee, unknown to Danish officials, aimed to use U.S. financial aid to replace Denmark's block grant, securing total U.S. military sovereignty over the island in exchange for supporting independence.

mainPoints.point: The U.S. has adopted the predatory tactics it once opposed, treating an ally as a target.
mainPoints.explanation: The article argues that the U.S. is now using influence operations and economic coercion against a NATO ally, mirroring the behavior of its traditional adversaries like China and Russia.

mainPoints.point: The threat is real: Danish forces are preparing for a potential U.S. military invasion.
mainPoints.explanation: The piece reports that Danish soldiers have been ordered to prepare to destroy Greenlandic runways to prevent a U.S. takeover, and the Danish Prime Minister has publicly stated that the post-WWII world order is over.

keyQuotes: If the United States chooses to attack another NATO country militarily, then everything comes to an end---including NATO and, with it, the security that has been provided since the end of the Second World War.
The world order as we know it---that we have been fighting for, for eighty years---is over, and I don't think it will return.
It is what it looks like---Trump is a king, and he's thinking about his empire. It's all about acquiring things---staking your claim, and then covering it in bling.

The reality is that the United States is now a country in which matters of war and peace are decided not among diplomatic or military experts, in the interests of the state, but through informal channels, by people whose personal proximity to the President---through family, business, donations, or flattery---is their principal qualification.

relatedArticles.title: Instead of Taking Your Job， A.I. Might Transform It
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article argues that AI is not primarily a job-replacing automation technology, but rather a tool that empowers workers to create bespoke, intern-like software, transforming their roles instead of eliminating them.

relatedArticles.title: Jensen Huang on TPU competition, selling chips to China, & Nvidia's supply chain moat
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: In this wide-ranging interview, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang articulates the company's core philosophy of 'converting electrons to tokens,' defends its CUDA ecosystem and supply chain moat against competitors like TPUs, and debates the strategic implications of U.S. export controls on China.

relatedArticles.title: Attacks On Data Centers， Qwen3.5 In All Sizes， DeepSeek’s Huawei Play， and more...
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This issue of The Batch discusses AI-driven job insecurity, the strategic targeting of data centers in modern warfare, and the release of Alibaba's Qwen3.5 vision-language models.

relatedArticles.title: On the Front Lines of Delaney Hall， ICE’s Newark Prison
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: A New Yorker dispatch from the front lines of the largest ICE detention center on the East Coast, capturing the daily protests, hunger strikes, and human stories that define the ongoing crisis.

relatedArticles.title: Ken Griffin’s Billions and Billions
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: A profile of Ken Griffin, the hedge-fund titan and founder of Citadel, exploring his immense wealth, business philosophy, political ambitions, and the public controversies surrounding his lifestyle.

relatedArticles.title: When Did White-Collar Work Start to Look So Bleak?
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article reviews three new books to trace the evolution of white-collar work from the aspirational yuppie era of the 1980s to the current climate of precarity and dread, linking the anxieties of today's graduates to historical shifts in corporate structure and economic promise.

relatedArticles.title: Jürgen Habermas Defended Reason in a Darkening Age
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article profiles Jürgen Habermas's life and philosophy, arguing that his defense of reason and the public sphere remains vital in an age of digital chaos and democratic backsliding.

relatedArticles.title: China Thwarts Meta’s Agentic Ambition， U.S. Evaluates Upcoming Models， AI Diagnoses Mammograms
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This issue of The Batch covers the U.S. government's new policy to evaluate AI models before public release, China blocking Meta's acquisition of the AI agent startup Manus, OpenAI's new speech-to-speech models, and a real-world study of Google's AI for mammogram diagnosis.

relatedArticles.title: Dario Amodei — Policy on the AI Exponential
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Dario Amodei argues that AI is advancing exponentially, creating a dangerous mismatch with slow-moving policy, and proposes concrete actions across regulation, economics, science, civil liberties, and geopolitics to meet the moment.

relatedArticles.title: The Next War Is Already Here. The West Isn't Ready. — Yaroslav Azhnyuk， The Fourth Law & Guest Host Noah Smith， Noahpinion
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This podcast episode with Yaroslav Azhnyuk, founder of The Fourth Law, argues that drone warfare, particularly FPV drones with AI autonomy, has fundamentally transformed modern battlefields, rendering traditional military platforms like tanks obsolete and exposing a widening gap between Western defense readiness and the reality of the war in Ukraine.
